Five candidates for young stellar objects have been detected as point sources for the first time in the 11<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>m image and it is suggested that that current star-formation has been triggered by previous star-formation activities. A wide area map of the size of about <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1^\circ$</tex> around the IC4954/4955 region was created from the AKARI mid-infrared All-Sky Survey data. Together with the H I 21 cm data, it suggests a large hollow structure of a degree scale, on whose edge the IC4954/4955 region has been created, indicating star formation over three generations in largely different spatial scales.

articleTitle: Observational Characteristics of the First Protostellar Cores
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: First protostellar cores are young stellar objects in the earliest evolutionary stage. They are hydrostatic objects formed soon after the central portions of star-forming cores become optically thick to dust emission. We consider their characteristics in the emitted radiation, and discuss their evolution with increasing mass of the cores. Particular attention is paid to detailed radiative and chemical processes in the postshock relaxation layer located at the surface of the core, where the majority of radiation is emitted. Most of the radiation is originally emitted in the dust continuum in mid-infrared wavelength (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 10–30 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m), which reprocessed to far-infrared with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 100–200 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m. Although some fraction (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 0.1) of the radiation energy is emitted in the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O lines at the accretion shock, most is absorbed and reemitted in the dust continuum in the envelope. The H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O lines account for at most <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1/100$</tex> of the observed luminosity. If a cavity is present in the envelope due to outflow or rotation, the dust and H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O line emission in the mid-infrared wavelength from the shock can be observed directly, or as a reflection nebula. Among forthcoming observational facillities, SPace Infrared telescope for Cosmology and Astrophysics (SPICA) is the most suitable for detecting either direct or processed radiation from first-core objects.

articleTitle: Spatial Distributions of Cold and Warm Interstellar Dust in M101 Resolved with AKARI/Far-Infrared Surveyor (FIS)
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The nearby face-on spiral galaxy M101 has been observed with the Far-Infrared Surveyor onboard AKARI. The far-infrared four-band images reveal fine spatial structures of M101, which include global spiral patterns, giant H II regions embedded in outer spiral arms, and a bar-like feature crossing the center. The spectral energy distribution of the whole galaxy shows the presence of a cold dust component (18<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+4}_{-10}$</tex>K) in addition to a warm dust component (55<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+9}_{-25}$</tex>K). The distribution of the cold dust is mostly concentrated near the center, and appears to be smoothly distributed over the entire extent of the galaxy, whereas the distribution of warm dust indicates some correlation with the spiral arms, and has spotty structures, such as four distinctive bright spots in the outer disk in addition to a bar-like feature near the center, tracing the CO intensity map. The star-formation activity of the giant H II regions that spatially correspond to the former bright spots is found to be significantly higher than that of the rest of the galaxy. The latter warm dust distribution implies that there are significant star-formation activities in the entire bar filled with molecular clouds. Unlike our Galaxy, M101 is a peculiar normal galaxy with extraordinary active star-forming regions.

articleTitle: Bispectrum and Nonlinear Biasing of Galaxies: Perturbation Analysis, Numerical Simulation, and SDSS Galaxy Clustering
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We consider nonlinear biasing models of galaxies with particular attention to a correlation between the linear and quadratic biasing coefficients, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_1$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_2$</tex>. We first derive perturbative expressions for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_1$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_2$</tex> in halo and peak biasing models. We then discuss our computations of the power spectra and bispectra of dark matter particles and halos using <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body simulation data and of volume-limited subsamples of Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) galaxies, and determine their <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_1$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_2$</tex>. We find that the values of those coefficients at linear regimes (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k<0.2$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$h$</tex> Mpc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>) are fairly insensitive to the redshift-space distortion and the survey volume shape. The resulting normalized amplitudes of the bispectra, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Q$</tex>, for equilateral triangles are insensitive to the values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_1$</tex>, implying that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_2$</tex> indeed correlates with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_1$</tex>. The present results explain the previous finding of Kayo et al. (2004, PASJ, 56, 415) for the hierarchical relation of three-point correlation functions of SDSS galaxies. While the relations between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_1$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$b_2$</tex> are quantitatively different for specific biasing models, their approximately similar correlations indicate a fairly generic outcome of the biasing due to the gravity in primordial Gaussian density fields.

articleTitle: Fundamental Parameters and Elemental Abundances of 160 F–G–K Stars Based on OAO Spectrum Database
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The properties of 160 F, G, and K disk dwarfs/subgiants (including 27 planet-host stars) mostly within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-0.6 \lesssim$</tex> [Fe/H] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim +0.4$</tex>, the Okayama Astrophysical Observatory spectrum collection of which had been made open to the public recently, were extensively investigated with particular attention to determining (1) the mass and the age with the help of theoretical stellar evolution calculations, (2) the kinematic parameters of orbital motions in the Galaxy, and (3) the abundances of 15 elements (Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Co, Ni, Cu, and Zn) by analyzing the spectra in this database. The resulting characteristics are discussed in terms of several relevant topics of interest, such as a validity check for assuming LTE, the [X/Fe] vs. [Fe/H] diagram containing information on the chemical evolution of the Galactic disk, the age–metallicity–kinematics relation, and the difference/similarity between stars with and without planets.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of the Local and Distant Hot ISM
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Suzaku observed the molecular cloud MBM 12 and a blank field less than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3^{\circ}$</tex> away to separate the local and distant components of the diffuse soft X-ray background. Towards MBM 12, a local (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D \lesssim 275 \,\mathrm{pc}$</tex>) O VII emission line was clearly detected with an intensity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.5 \;\mathrm{photons} \;\mathrm{cm}^{-2} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1} \,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$</tex> (or line units, LU), and the O VIII flux was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${<0.34 \;\mathrm{LU}}$</tex>. The origin of this O VII emission could be hot gas in the Local Hot Bubble (LHB), charge exchange within the heliosphere with oxygen ions from the solar wind (SWCX), or both. If entirely from the LHB, the emission could be explained by a region with emission measure of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.0075 \,\mathrm{cm}^{-6} \,\mathrm{pc}$</tex> and a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.2 \times 10^6 \,\mathrm{K}$</tex>. However, this temperature and emission measure implies <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1/4 \;\mathrm{keV}$</tex> emission in excess of observations. There is no evidence in the X-ray light curve or solar wind data for a significant contribution from geocoronal SWCX, although interplanetary SWCX is still possible. In any case, the observed O VII flux represents an upper limit to both the LHB emission and interplanetary SWCX in this direction. The blank field was observed immediately afterwards. The net off-cloud O VII and O VIII intensities were (respectively) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.34 \pm 0.33$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.77 \pm 0.16 \;\mathrm{LU}$</tex>, after subtracting the on-cloud foreground emission. If this more distant O VII and O VIII emission is from a thermal plasma in collisional equilibrium beyond the Galactic disk, we infer it has a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(2.1 \pm 0.1) \times 10^6 \,\mathrm{K}$</tex> with an emission measure of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(4 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-3} \,\mathrm{cm}^{-6} \,\mathrm{pc}$</tex>.

articleTitle: The IRSF Magellanic Clouds Point Source Catalog
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a near-infrared (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$JHK_{\rm s}$</tex>) photometric catalog, including 14811185 point sources for a 40 deg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> area of the Large Magellanic Cloud, 2769682 sources for an 11 deg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> area of the Small Magellanic Cloud, and 434145 sources for a 4 deg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> area of the Magellanic Bridge. The 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex> limiting magnitudes are 18.8, 17.8, and 16.6 mag at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J, H$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\rm s}$</tex>, respectively. The photometric and astrometric accuracies for bright sources are 0.03–0.04 mag and 0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rlap {.}{^{\prime\prime}}$</tex>1, respectively. Based on the catalog, we also present (1) spatial distributions, (2) luminosity functions, (3) color–color diagrams, and (4) color–magnitude diagrams for point sources toward the Magellanic Clouds.

articleTitle: Characteristic Scales of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations from Perturbation Theory: Nonlinearity and Redshift-Space Distortion Effects
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: An acoustic oscillation of the primeval photon-baryon fluid around the decoupling time imprints a characteristic scale in the galaxy distribution today, known as the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) scale. Several ongoing and/or future galaxy surveys aim to detect and precisely determine the BAO scale so as to trace the expansion history of the universe. We consider nonlinear and redshift-space distortion effects on the shifts of the BAO scale in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k$</tex>-space using perturbation theory. The resulting shifts are indeed sensitive to different choices for the definition of the BAO scale, which needs to be kept in mind in the data analysis. We present a toy model to explain the physical behavior of the shifts. We find that the BAO scale defined as in Percival et al. (2007, ApJ, 657, 51) indeed shows very small shifts (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex>1%) relative to the prediction in linear theory in real space. The shifts can be predicted accurately for scales where perturbation theory is reliable.

articleTitle: Multi-Slit Imaging Spectroscopy Technique: Catalog of Intracluster Planetary Nebulae in the Coma Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: With a new multi-slit imaging spectroscopy (MSIS) technique pioneered at the 8.2 m Subaru telescope and the Faint Object Camera and Spectrograph, we detect and measure the line-of-sight velocities of 40 intracluster planetary nebula candidates associated with the diffuse intracluster population of stars in the Coma cluster core, at nearly 100 Mpc distance. We describe the method for extracting the single two-dimensional spectra from the MSIS image, discuss the criteria for the identification of the emission line objects, and describe the procedure to compute their <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha, \delta$</tex> (J2000) coordinates. We present the catalog of the intracluster planetary nebula candidates, their spatial location in the surveyed field, and their distribution in the velocity–magnitude plane. Finally, we comment on possible population effects and the use of these planetary nebulae to confirm the distance to the Coma cluster.

articleTitle: Infrared Camera (IRC) Deep Survey in the Performance-Verification Phase
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the first results of a near- and mid-infrared deep survey with the Infrared Camera (IRC) onboard AKARI in the performance-verification phase. Simultaneous observations by the Near-InfraRed (NIR), Mid-InfraRed Short (MIR-S), and Mid-InfraRed Long (MIR-L) channels of the IRC with effective integration times of 4529, 4908, and 4417 seconds at 3, 7, and 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>m, covering 86.0, 70.3, and 77.3 arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> area, detected 955, 298, and 277 sources, respectively. The 5 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex> detection limits of the survey are 6.0, 31.5, and 71.2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>Jy and the 50% completeness limit are 24.0, 47.5, and 88.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>Jy at 3, 7, and 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>m, respectively. Observation are limited by source confusion at 3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>m. We have confirmed the turnover in the 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>m differential source counts around 400<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>Jy, previously detected by surveys with the Infrared Space Observatory. The faint end of 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>m raw source counts agrees with those from deep surveys in the GOODS fields, carried out with the Spitzer IRS peak up imager and predictions of current galaxy evolution models. These results indicate that deep surveys with comprehensive wavelength coverage at mid-infrared wavelength are very important to investigate the evolution of infrared galaxies at high redshifts.

articleTitle: Formation Process of a Light Bridge Revealed with the Hinode Solar Optical Telescope
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) on-board Hinode successfully and continuously observed the formation process of a light bridge in a matured sunspot of the NOAA active region 10923 for several days with high spatial resolution. During its formation, many umbral dots were observed to be emerging from the leading edges of penumbral filaments, and rapidly intruding into the umbra. The precursor of the light bridge formation was also identified as a relatively slow inward motion of the umbral dots, which emerged not near the penumbra, but inside the umbra. The spectro-polarimeter on SOT provided physical conditions in the photosphere around the umbral dots and the light bridges. We found that the light bridges and the umbral dots had significantly weaker magnetic fields associated with upflows relative to the core of the umbra, which implies that there was hot gas with weak field strength penetrating from the subphotosphere to near the visible surface inside those structures. There needs to be a mechanism to drive the inward motion of the hot gas along the light bridges. We suggest that the emergence and the inward motion are triggered by a buoyant penumbral flux tube as well as subphotospheric flow crossing the sunspot.

articleTitle: Missing Dwarf Problem in Galaxy Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigated the formation and evolution of CDM subhalos in galaxy-sized and cluster-sized halos by means of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body simulations. Our aim was to make clear what the “dwarf galaxy problem” is. It has been argued that the number of subhalos in simulated galaxy-sized halos is too large compared with the observed number of dwarfs in the local group, while that in cluster-sized halos is consistent with the observed number of galaxies in clusters, such as the Virgo cluster. We simulated nine halos with several different mass resolutions and physical scales. We found that the dependence of the cumulative number of subhalos, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_c$</tex>, on their maximum circular velocity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_c$</tex>, is given by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_c\propto V_c^{-3}$</tex>, down to the reliability limit, independent of the mass of the main halo. This implies that simulations for cluster-sized halos give too many halos with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_c \sim$</tex>140 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> or less. Previous comparisons of cluster-sized halos gave a much smaller number of subhalos in this regime, simply because of their limited resolution. Our result implies that any theory that attempts to resolve the missing dwarf problem should also explain the discrepancy of the simulation and observation in cluster-sized halos.

articleTitle: Optical Identification of 15$\mu $m Sources in the AKARI Performance Verification Field toward the North Ecliptic Pole
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of optical identifications for 257 mid-infrared sources detected with a deep 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m survey over approximately 80 arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> area in the AKARI performance verification field near the North Ecliptic Pole. The 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m fluxes of the sources range from 1 mJy down to 40 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>Jy, approximately one half of which are below 100 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu $</tex>Jy. Optical counterparts were searched for within a 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime\prime}$</tex>-3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime\prime}$</tex> radius in both the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$BVRi'z'$</tex> catalog generated by using the deep Subaru/Suprime-cam field, which covers one-third of the performance verification field, and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$g'r'i'z'$</tex> catalog based on observations made with MegaCam at CFHT. We found that the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B-R$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R-z'$</tex> colors of sources with successful optical identifications are systematically redder than that of the entire optical sample in the same field. Moreover, approximately 40% of the 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m sources show colors with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R-$</tex>L15 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 5, which cannot be explained by the spectral energy distribution (SED) of normal quiescent spiral galaxies, but are consistent with SEDs of redshifted (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z>1$</tex>) starburst or ultraluminous infrared galaxies. This result indicates that the fraction of the ultraluminous infrared galaxies in our faint 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m sample is much larger than that in our brighter 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m sources, which is consistent with the evolving mid-infrared luminosity function derived by recent studies based on Spitzer 24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m deep surveys. Based on an SED fitting technique, the nature of the faint 15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\mu$</tex>m sources is further discussed for a selected number of sources with available <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K_{\rm s}$</tex>-band data.

articleTitle: Steady Models of Optically Thin, Magnetically Supported Black Hole Accretion Disks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We obtained steady solutions of optically thin, single-temperature, magnetized black hole accretion disks, assuming thermal bremsstrahlung cooling. Based on the results of 3D MHD simulations of accretion disks, we assumed that the magnetic fields inside the disk are turbulent and dominated by an azimuthal component. We decomposed the magnetic fields into an azimuthally averaged mean field and fluctuating fields. We also assumed that the azimuthally averaged Maxwell stress is proportional to the total pressure. The radial advection rate of the azimuthal magnetic flux, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot \Phi$</tex>, is prescribed as being proportional to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\varpi^{-\zeta}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\varpi$</tex> is the radial coordinate and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\zeta$</tex> is a parameter that parameterizes the radial variation of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot \Phi$</tex>. We found that when the accretion rate, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot M$</tex>, exceeds the threshold for the onset of the thermal instability, a magnetic pressure-dominated new branch appears. Thus, the thermal-equilibrium curve of an optically thin disk has a ‘Z’-shape in the plane of the surface density and temperature. This indicates that as the mass accretion rate increases, a gas pressure-dominated optically thin hot accretion disk undergoes a transition to a magnetic pressure dominated, optically thin cool disk. This disk corresponds to the X-ray hard, luminous disk in black hole candidates observed during the transition from a low/hard state to a high/soft state. We also obtained global steady transonic solutions containing such a transition layer.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of HESS J1616—508: Evidence for a Dark Particle Accelerator
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We observed the bright unidentified TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray source HESS J1616-508 with the X-ray Imaging Spectrometers onboard the Suzaku satellite. No X-ray counterpart was found to a limiting flux of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.1 \times 10^{-13} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1} \,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$</tex> in the 2–10 keV band, which is some 60-times below the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-ray flux in the 1–10TeV band. This object is bright in TeV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>-rays, but very dim in the X-ray band, and thus is one of the best examples in the Galaxy of a “dark particle accelerator.” We also detected soft thermal emission with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT \sim 0.3 \hbox{--} 0.6 \,\mathrm{keV}$</tex> near the location of HESS J1616-508. This may be due to a dust-grain scattering halo from the nearby bright supernova remnant RCW 103.

articleTitle: Suzaku Spectroscopic Study of Hard X-Ray Emission in the Arches Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of a Suzaku study of the Arches cluster in the Galactic center region. A high signal-to-noise ratio spectrum in the 3–12 keV band was obtained with the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) onboard the Suzaku observatory. We found that the spectrum consists of a thermal plasma, a hard power-law tail, and two Gaussian line components. The plasma component with a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 2.2 \,\mathrm{keV}$</tex> is established from the presence of Ca XIX and Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> lines as well as absence of the Fe XXVI <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> line. The two Gaussian lines represent the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\beta$</tex> lines from iron at lower ionization stages at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 6.4$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 7.1 \,\mathrm{keV}$</tex>. Both the line centers and the intensity ratio of these two lines are consistent with neutral iron. The hard power-law tail with a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.7$</tex> was found to have no pronounced iron K edge feature. Compared with the published Chandra spectra constructed separately for point-like and diffuse emission, we conclude that the thermal component is from an ensemble of point-like sources plus thermal diffuse emission concentrated at the cluster center, while the Gaussian and the hard tail components are from non-thermal diffuse emission extended in a larger scale. In band-limited images of the XIS field, the distribution of the 7.5–10.0 keV emission resembles that of the 6.4 keV emission, including local excess at the Arches cluster. This strongly suggests that the power-law emission is related to the 6.4 and 7.1 keV lines in the underlying physics. We discuss two ideas to explain both the hard continuum and the lines: (1) X-ray photoionization that produces fluorescence lines and the Thomson scattering continuum and (2) non-thermal electron impact ionization of iron atoms and bremsstrahlung continuum. However, whichever scenario is adopted, the photon or particle flux from the Arches cluster is too low to account for the observed lines and continuum intensity.

articleTitle: Astrometry of Galactic Star-Forming Region Sharpless 269 with VERA: Parallax Measurements and Constraint on Outer Rotation Curve
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have performed high-precision astrometry of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser sources in the Galactic star-forming region Sharpless 269 (S269) with VERA. We successfully detected a trigonometric parallax of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$189 \pm 8 \mu$</tex>as, corresponding to a source distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$5.28^{+0.24}_{-0.22}$</tex> kpc. This is the smallest parallax ever measured, and the first one detected beyond 5 kpc. The source distance as well as the proper motions were used to constrain the outer rotation curve of the Galaxy, demonstrating that the difference of rotation velocities at the Sun and at S269 (which is 13.1 kpc away from the Galaxy’s center) is less than 3%. This gives the strongest constraint on the flatness of the outer rotation curve, and provides a direct confirmation of the existence of a large amount of dark matter in the Galaxy’s outer disk.

articleTitle: Infrared Spectroscopy of Short-Period Cataclysmic Variables
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present near-infrared spectra for five dwarf novae with short orbital periods. We performed fittings of the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) by assuming a power-law distribution for the accretion disk and using template spectra of late-type dwarfs for the secondary star. Two are WZ Sge–or WX Cet-type stars, whose spectra show water absorption features, and one of them shows K I and Na I absorption lines in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>-band. We find that the secondary contributions to the overall SED are larger in WZ Sge stars than in ER UMa stars. The SED fitting suggests M9 and L1 type dwarf companions for our WZ Sge systems, and an M2 dwarf for our ER UMa star. We discuss the direct relationship between the high temperatures of secondary stars and high mass-transfer rates in ER UMa stars. SDSS J013701.06–091234.9 is the only object showing a spectrum dominated by the secondary component. The spectrum strongly suggests that the evolutionary path of SDSS J013701.06–091234.9 is different from that of ordinary CVs, and this object is a candidate of EI Psc-like systems.

Author Keywords: stars: individual (ASAS 002511+1217.2, IX Draconis, SDSS J013701.06–091234.9, V1108 Hercles, V503 Cygni)

articleTitle: Subaru Near-Infrared Multicolor Images of Class II Young Stellar Object, RNO 91
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We conducted subarcsecond near-infrared imaging observations of RNO 91 with CIAO (Coronagraphic Imager with Adaptive Optics) mounted on the 8.2 m Subaru telescope. We present our JHK band data along with optical images, which when considered together reveal a complex circumstellar structure. We examined the colors of associated nebulae and compared the geometry of the outflow/disk system suggested by our data with that already proposed on the basis of previous studies. Our K-band image shows bright circumstellar nebulosity detected within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime\prime}$</tex> around the central source, while it is less conspicuous at shorter wavelengths. PA and the size of this red color nebulosity agree with those of the previously detected polarization disk. Agreements among these data indicate that this bright nebulosity region, which follows the reddening law, might be attributed to a disklike structure. At <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex> and optical wavelengths, several blue knotlike structures are detected around and beyond the bright circumstellar nebulosity. We suggest that these knotty reflection nebulae may represent disintegrating fragments of an infalling envelope. The three-color composite image has the appearance of arc-shaped nebulosity. We interpret these structures as being roots of a bipolar cavity opening toward the northeast and the southwest. The complex distribution of reflection nebulosity seen around RNO 91 appears to confirm the interpretation that this source is an object dispersing its molecular envelope while transitioning from protostar to T Tauri star.

articleTitle: Iron and Nickel Line Diagnostics for the Galactic Center Diffuse Emission
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have observed the diffuse X-ray emission from the Galactic Center (GC) using the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) on Suzaku. The high-energy resolution and the low-background orbit provided excellent spectra of the GC diffuse X-rays (GCDX). The XIS found many emission lines in the GCDX near the energy of K-shell transitions of iron and nickel. The most pronounced features are Fe I <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> at 6.4 keV and K-shell absorption edge at 7.1 keV, which are from neutral and/or low ionization states of iron, and the K-shell lines at 6.7 keV and 6.9 keV from He-like (Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex>) and hydrogenic (Fe XXVI Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>) ions of iron. In addition, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> lines from neutral or low ionization nickel (Ni I <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex>) and He-like nickel (Ni XXVII <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex>), Fe I <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\beta$</tex>, Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\beta$</tex>, Fe XXVI <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Ly}\beta$</tex>, Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\gamma$</tex>, and Fe XXVI <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Ly}\gamma$</tex> were detected for the first time. The line center energies and widths of Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> and Fe XXVI <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Ly}\alpha$</tex> favor a collisional excitation plasma for the origin of the GCDX. The electron temperature determined from the line flux ratio of Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex>/ Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\beta$</tex> is similar to the ionization temperature determined from that of Fe XXV <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex>/ Fe XXVI <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Ly}\alpha$</tex>. Thus it would appear that the GCDX plasma is close to ionization equilibrium. The 6.7 keV flux and temperature distribution to the galactic longitude is smooth and monotonic, in contrast to the integrated point source flux distribution. These facts support the hypothesis that the GCDX is truly diffuse emission rather than the integration of the outputs of a large number of unresolved point sources. In addition, our results demonstrate that the chemical composition of Fe in the interstellar gas near the GC is constrained to be about 3.5 times solar abundance.

articleTitle: Abundances of Volatile Elements in Post-AGB Candidates
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A detailed non-LTE study on the abundances of C, N, O, S, and Zn was carried out for five F–G supergiants of suspected post-AGB candidates with IR excesses (HD 112374, HD 148743, HD 161796, HD 163506, and HD 187203), since these volatile elements can provide the key to inferring the original metallicity as well as an evolution-induced change due to mixing, given that they are free from depletion caused by dust–gas separation. The extent of separation-induced depletion in Fe, estimated by comparing with Zn, turned out to be rather moderate (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lesssim$</tex> several tenths dex). The characteristics of the C, N, and O abundances do not appear to be very different from the case of the first dredge-up in normal supergiants (decreased C and enriched N due to the first dredge-up); thus, the specific anomaly related to an advanced post-AGB stage so far reported (such as elevated C and O) could not be clearly confirmed.

Author Keywords: stars: individual (HD 112374, HD 148743, HD 161796, HD 163506, HD 187203)

articleTitle: X-Ray Spectral Study of the Extended Emission, ‘the Cap’, Located 11.6 kpc above the Disk of M82
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The extended X-ray emission from ‘the Cap’ region, located <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$11{}^{\prime }$</tex> (11.6 kpc) above the disk of the starburst galaxy M82, has been observed with Suzaku and XMM-Newton. Owing to the good energy resolution and the large collecting area of the XIS on Suzaku, combined with similar properties of the EPIC instrument on XMM-Newton, we have clearly detected K-shell emission lines from O VII, O VIII, Ne X, Mg XI, Mg XII, Sr XIII, and the Fe L complex. Two optically thin thermal plasma components are required to fit the observed X-ray spectra. We have determined the metal abundances of O, Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe in this region for the first time. Their metal abundance ratios agree well with those of metal-poor stars and the model prediction of metals synthesized by type-II supernovae, but they are not consistent with the metallicities of type-Ia supernovae. This result is support for the idea that the origin of the metals in the Cap is type-II supernova explosions occurring in the starburst regions in the M82 galaxy. We discuss the possible contribution from sputtered dust grains to the metals in the Cap. An emission line consistent with the C VI transition of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n=4$</tex> to 1 at 0.459 keV has been marginally detected, although it is not statistically significant at the 99% confidence level; the presence of this line would suggest charge-exchange processes in the Cap.

Index Terms: Center Of The Field Of View

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of the Metallicity Distribution in the Intracluster Medium of the Fornax Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The metallicity distribution in the Fornax cluster was studied with the XIS instrument on board the Suzaku satellite. The K-shell lines of O and Mg were resolved clearly, and the abundances of O, Mg, Si, S, and Fe were measured with great accuracy. The region within a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4'$</tex> radius of NGC 1399 shows approximately solar abundances of Fe, Si, and S, while the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{O/Fe}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Mg/Fe}$</tex> abundance ratios are about 0.4–0.5 and 0.7 in solar units, respectively. In the outer region of the radius range <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$6' < r < 23'$</tex>, the Fe and Si abundances drop to 0.4–0.5 solar and show no significant gradient within this region. The abundance ratios, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{O/Fe}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{Mg/Fe}$</tex>, are consistent with those in the central region. We also measured the Fe abundance around NGC 1404 to be approximately solar, and the O, Ne, and Mg abundances to be 0.5–0.7 times the Fe level. A significant relative enhancement of Fe within 130 kpc of NGC 1399 and in NGC 1404 indicates an origin in SN Ia, in contrast to the species O, Ne, and Mg, which reflect the stellar metallicity. The mass-to-light ratios for O and Fe within 130 kpc of NGC 1399 are over an order of magnitude lower than those in rich clusters, reflecting the metal enrichment history of this poor cluster.

articleTitle: Revealing the High Energy Emission from the Obscured Seyfert Galaxy MCG−5–23–16 with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on a 100 ks Suzaku observation of the bright, nearby (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=0.008486$</tex>) Seyfert 1.9 galaxy MCG -5–23–16. The broad-band (0.4–100 keV) X-ray spectrum allows us to determine the nature of the high energy emission with little ambiguity. The X-ray continuum consists of a cutoff power-law of photon index <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma=1.9$</tex>, absorbed through Compton-thin matter of column density <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\mathrm{H}} = 1.6 \times 10^{22} \,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$</tex>. A soft excess is observed below 1 keV and is likely a combination of emission from scattered continuum photons and distant photoionized gas. The iron K line profile is complex, showing narrow neutral iron <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\alpha$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{K}\beta$</tex> emission, as well as a broad line which can be modeled by a moderately inclined accretion disk. The line profile shows either the disk is truncated at a few tens of gravitational radii, or the disk emissivity profile is relatively flat. A strong Compton reflection component is detected above 10 keV, which is best modeled by a combination of reflection off distant matter and the accretion disk. The reflection component does not appear to vary. The overall picture is that this Seyfert 1.9 galaxy is viewed at moderate (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 50^\circ$</tex>) inclination through Compton-thin matter at the edge of a Compton-thick torus covering <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 2\pi$</tex> steradians, consistent with unified models.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of the Centaurus Cluster: Absence of Bulk Motions in the Intracluster Medium
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The Centaurus cluster (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=0.0104$</tex>) was observed with the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) onboard the Suzaku X-ray satellite in three pointings, one centered on the cluster core and the other two offset by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm 8 {{}^{\prime }}$</tex> in declination. To search for possible bulk motions of the intracluster medium, the central energy of a He-like Fe K line (at a rest-frame energy of 6.7 kev) was examined to look for a positional dependence. Over spatial scales of 50 kpc to 140 kpc around the cluster core, the central line energy was found to be constant within a calibration error of 15 eV. The 90% upper limit on the line-of-sight velocity difference is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert\Delta v\vert < 1400 \,\mathrm{km} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, giving a tighter constraint than previous measurements. The significant velocity gradients inferred from a previous Chandra study were not detected between two pairs of rectangular regions near the cluster core. These results suggest that the bulk velocity does not largely exceed the thermal velocity of the gas in the central region of the Centaurus cluster. The mean redshift of the intracluster medium was determined to be 0.0097, in agreement with the optical redshift of the cluster within the calibration uncertainty. Implications of the present results for estimating the cluster mass are briefly discussed.

articleTitle: Flight Performance of the AKARI Cryogenic System
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We describe the flight performance of the cryogenic system of the infrared astronomical satellite AKARI, which was successfully launched on 2006 February 21 (UT). AKARI carries a 68.5 cm telescope together with two focal-plane instruments, Infrared Cameras and Far Infrared Surveyor, all of which are cooled down to cryogenic temperature to achieve superior sensitivity. AKARI has a unique cryogenic system, which consists of cryogen (liquid helium) and mechanical coolers (2-stage Stirling coolers). With the help of mechanical coolers, 179 L (26.0 kg) of super-fluid liquid helium can keep the instruments cryogenically cooled for more than 500 days. The on-orbit performance of the AKARI cryogenics is consistent with the design and a pre-flight test, and the boil-off gas flow rate is as small as 0.32 mg s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. We observed an increase in the major axis of the AKARI orbit, which can be explained by thrust due to the thermal pressure of vented helium gas.

articleTitle: Subsystems in a Stable Planetary System
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Our planetary system is dynamically stable for the lifetime of the Sun according to long-term numerical integrations of the planetary orbits (2002, MNRAS, 336, 483). We first list up possible subsystems of a stable planetary system, and then discuss three forms of subsystems that may contribute to maintaining the stability of the system, and whose role may have escaped analysis by dynamical astronomers. We stress that multiplanet subsystems may have a variety of mechanisms for maintaining stability. This is in contrast with the stability problem of massless bodies, such as asteroids, satellites, and comets.

Author Keywords: planets and satellites: dynamical evolution and stability

articleTitle: Polarimetric Imager for Comets, PICO
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We constructed an imaging polarimeter, PICO, that was optimized for comets and/or cometary objects. PICO has a field-of-view of 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$' \times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$'$</tex> and employs a fixed Wollaston prism as an analyzer. In the case of polarimeters using a double-beam prism, such as a Wollaston prism, lateral chromatic aberrations originating from the prism often degrade the image quality and measurement accuracy. However, PICO suffers little lateral chromatic aberration due to compensation provided by newly designed lens systems that generate opposite lateral colors. Owing to this design, PICO can obtain highly resolved and very accurate polarization images throughout the FOV (field-of-view). The total accuracy is estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta P \simeq [(P/8{5})^2 + 0.3^2]^{1/2}\;$</tex>% in polarization degree and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\theta \leq$</tex> 3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> in position angle; these values are satisfactory for cometary studies.
